claim: Heart valve defects are common congenital cardiac malformations in humans
source: Heart valve development is a great model for studying these interactions when considering that heart valve defects are common congenital cardiac malformation in human (Hoffman and Kaplan, 2002; Øyen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffman and Kaplan, 2002 and Øyen et al., 2009

claim: The four-chambered heart contains two different sets of valves
source: The four-chambered heart contains two different sets of valves (Lin et al., 2012):
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2012

claim: Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital malformation of arterial valve leaflets
source: Abnormalities of the arterial valve leaflets are the most-common congenital malformations, in particular bicuspid aortic valve (Hoffman and Kaplan, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoffman and Kaplan, 2002

claim: Aortic valves mainly derive from endocardial cushion progenitors with potential contribution from epicardial cells and neural crest
source: Aortic valves mainly derive from endocardial cushion progenitors with a potential contribution from other cellular sources (epicardial cells and neural crest) (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2017

claim: Valve formation depends on cell proliferation mediated by the vegf-nfat1 pathway
source: Generally, valve formation depends on two main events: cell proliferation, which is mainly mediated by the vegf-nfat1 pathway, matrix deposition and an endothelial-to-mesenchymal transformation (endMT) under the control of Gata transcription factors (Laforest et al., 2011; Stefanovic et al., 2014), Notch signaling (Luxán et al., 2016), Smad/tgf-beta/Bmp, and Wnt-beta catenin signals (Combs and Yutzey, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laforest et al., 2011; Stefanovic et al., 2014; Luxán et al., 2016; Combs and Yutzey, 2009

claim: Arterial valves develop differently from atrioventricular valves by differentiating directly from progenitors in the outflow wall independently from endMT in mouse
source: Nevertheless, recent evidence suggests that arterial valves develop differently from atrioventricular valves by differentiating directly from progenitors in the outflow wall independently from endMT in mouse (Eley et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eley et al., 2018

claim: Aortic valves are located in areas of high flow velocity
source: Aortic valves are located in areas of high flow velocity and mechanical forces have a great impact on valve morphogenesis (Butcher et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Butcher et al., 2008

claim: Abnormal blood circulation is a cardiovascular risk factor
source: Abnormal blood circulation is widely recognized as a cardiovascular risk factor and abnormal mechanotransduction has been associated with valvulopathies (Bäck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bäck et al., 2013

claim: Congenital heart valve malformations are associated with genetic mutations in genes essential for heart valve development
source: Congenital heart valve malformations are usually associated with genetic mutations in genes essential for heart valve development, such as signaling factors (Notch1, TGFβ) for the aortic valves (Bäck et al., 2013), and actin-binding proteins (FilaminA) for the mitral valves (Sauls et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bäck et al., 2013 and Sauls et al., 2012

claim: Genetic mutations linking valve defects with genes involved in controlling developmental programs have been discovered
source: The reoccurring discovery of genetic mutations linking valve defects with genes involved in controlling developmental programs (e.g., in NOTCH1, TBX5, GATA4, TBX20, LMCD1, TNS1, and DCHS1) (PROMESA investigators et al., 2015; Durst et al., 2015; Garg et al., 2005; Richards and Garg, 2010), has spurred interest in valve morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to PROMESA investigators et al., 2015; Durst et al., 2015; Garg et al., 2005; Richards and Garg, 2010

claim: The zebrafish heart is two chambered and contains three sets of valves
source: Zebrafish heart is two chambered and contains three sets of valves (the outflow tract (OFT), atrioventricular (AVC) and the inflow tract (IFT) valve [Figure 1A]) that are all bicuspid (Beis et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2019; Tessadori et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beis et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2019; Tessadori et al., 2012

claim: Zebrafish heart valves originate from progenitors located in the ventricle and atrium
source: Zebrafish heart valves originate from progenitors located in the ventricle and atrium that generate the valve leaflets through a coordinated set of endocardial tissue movements (Boselli et al., 2017; Pestel et al., 2016; Steed et al., 2016a; Steed et al., 2016b; Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boselli et al., 2017; Pestel et al., 2016; Steed et al., 2016a; Steed et al., 2016b; Vermot et al., 2009

claim: In the zebrafish AVC, blood flow and Klf2a control notch1b and bmp4 expression, both necessary for valve formation
source: In the zebrafish AVC, blood flow and Klf2a control notch1b and bmp4 expression, both of which are necessary for valve formation (Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vermot et al., 2009

claim: Klf2a regulates the deposition of matrix protein (in particular Fibronectin1) in the valve forming area
source: Klf2a regulates the deposition of matrix protein (in particular Fibronectin1) in the valve forming area (Steed et al., 2016b), as well as Wnt signaling by controlling wnt9b expression (Goddard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steed et al., 2016b and Goddard et al., 2017

claim: Canonical Wnt signals arise specifically in sub-endocardial, abluminal cells and are dependent upon hemodynamic forces in zebrafish
source: The latter is consistent with the fact that canonical Wnt signals arise specifically in sub-endocardial, abluminal cells and that these Wnt signals are dependent upon hemodynamic forces in zebrafish (Pestel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pestel et al., 2016

claim: Notch signaling is essential for aortic valve formation
source: In addition, Notch signaling is essential for aortic valve formation (Garg, 2016) and OFT development (MacGrogan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garg, 2016; MacGrogan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017

claim: Fluid shear stress is an important environmental cue that governs vascular physiology and pathology
source: Fluid shear stress is an important environmental cue that governs vascular physiology and pathology (Baeyens et al., 2016), but the molecular mechanisms that mediate endocardial responses to flow are only partially understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to Baeyens et al., 2016

claim: In zebrafish, the mechanosensitive channels Trpv4 and Trpp2 modulate endocardial calcium signaling and klf2a expression necessary for valve morphogenesis
source: In zebrafish, the mechanosensitive channels Trpv4 and Trpp2 modulate endocardial calcium signaling and klf2a expression is necessary for valve morphogenesis and downstream pathway activation (Heckel et al., 2015; Steed et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heckel et al., 2015 and Steed et al., 2016b

claim: Notch signaling is tightly involved in cellular mechanosensitive responses in human aortic valves
source: Notch signaling is tightly involved in cellular mechanosensitive responses in human aortic valves (Godby et al., 2014) and Notch1 is a potent mechanosensor in adult arteries (Mack et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Godby et al., 2014 and Mack et al., 2017

claim: Stretch-sensitive channels from the Piezo family are important for vascular development
source: More recently, it has been shown that stretch-sensitive channels from the Piezo family (Murthy et al., 2017) are important for vascular development (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014) and lymphatic valve formation (Nonomura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murthy et al., 2017; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014; Nonomura et al., 2018

claim: Piezo channels exert essential roles during cell differentiation in the embryo
source: In the embryo, Piezo channels exert essential roles during cell differentiation (He et al., 2018) and can affect lineage choice by modulating the nuclear localization of the mechanoreactive transcription coactivator Yap (Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to He et al., 2018 and Pathak et al., 2014

claim: The BA dampens the pressure wave down the arterial tree
source: The BA dampens the pressure wave down the arterial tree (Braun et al., 2003b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Braun et al., 2003b

claim: The BA expresses elastic fiber genes that provide mechanical properties necessary for its physiological function
source: To perform its function, the BA expresses elastic fiber genes that are thought to provide the mechanical properties necessary for its physiological function (Braun et al., 2003a; Braun et al., 2003b; Keith et al., 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 2003a; Braun et al., 2003b; Keith et al., 1977

claim: Elastin b contributes to the development of the BA by regulating cell fate determination of cardiac precursor cells into smooth muscle via a process involving Yap1
source: The extracellular matrix (ECM) gene, elastin b, contributes to the development of the BA by regulating cell fate determination of cardiac precursor cells into smooth muscle via a process that involves the mechanotransducer Yap1 (Moriyama et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moriyama et al., 2016

claim: Blood flow in the OFT is bidirectional until functional valve leaflets emerge at 144 hpf
source: Live imaging of the double transgenic line Tg(gata1:ds-red; kdrl:EGFP) to follow red blood cells and endothelial cell wall movements reveal dramatic changes in intracardiac blood flow patterns during OFT valve development: as the heart matures, blood flow in the OFT is bidirectional until functional valve leaflets emerge in the OFT at 144 hpf (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from live imaging and Figure 1A-C

claim: The periods within the cardiac cycle in which reversing flow can be observed decrease in length until 144 hpf
source: Throughout development, the periods within the cardiac cycle in which reversing flow can be observed decrease in length until 144 hpf, the stage at which we could not observe reversing flow anymore (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 1C

claim: At 56 hpf, the endothelium resembles a tube, maturing into cushions by 72 hpf, into premature leaflets by 96 hpf and finally into elongated, thin leaflets by 144 hpf
source: Using the Tg(fli:lifeact-EGFP; kdrl:nls-mCherry) line, which labels endothelial cells, we found that these flow profile modifications are linked to changes in OFT tissue geometry and the state of OFT maturation (Figure 1B). At 56 hpf, the endothelium resembles a tube (Figure 1B,C), maturing into cushions by 72 hpf, into premature leaflets by 96 hpf and finally into elongated, thin leaflets by 144 hpf (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transgenic line imaging and Figure 1B,C

claim: The endothelium folds to form the valve without multilayering
source: The results suggest that the endothelium folds to form the valve without multilayering (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Photoconverted cells remain attached to each other and do not show signs of delamination as observed in the AVC
source: Indeed, we could observe that the photoconverted cells remain attached to each other and do not show signs of delamination as observed in the AVC (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: At 72 hpf, cushions appear and Fn1 is observed in the cells around the endothelial cells, that are themselves surrounded at their base by myocardium in the posterior part
source: At 72 hpf, cushions appear and Fn1 is observed in the cells around the endothelial cells, that are themselves surrounded at their base by myocardium in the posterior part (Figure 3A,B,C,D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A,B,C,D,E

claim: Fn1 expression level increases at 96 hpf and delineates a group of cells surrounding the OFT as well as in the basal side of a few endothelial cells that form the cushions
source: Fn1 expression level increases at 96 hpf and delineates a group of cells surrounding the OFT as well as in the basal side of a few endothelial cells that form the cushions (Figure 3C, arrows, E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C,E

claim: In the developed leaflets at 120 hpf, Fn1 expression is maintained within the leaflets
source: In the developed leaflets at 120 hpf, Fn1 expression is maintained within the leaflets (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: Most of the cells surrounding the endothelium expressing Fn1 also express Elastin b (Elnb), a marker of smooth muscle cells
source: We found that most of the cells surrounding the endothelium expressing Fn1 also express Elastin b (Elnb, Eln2 or Tropoelastin), a marker of smooth muscle cells (Grimes et al., 2006; Miao et al., 2007; Paffett-Lugassy et al., 2017) (Figure 3B', C', D').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B', C', D' and citations to Grimes et al., 2006; Miao et al., 2007; Paffett-Lugassy et al., 2017

claim: The cells surrounding the Fn1 cells are not myocardial cells as the myocardium stops just before the BA region
source: We could confirm that the cells surrounding the Fn1 cells are not myocardial cells as the myocardium stops just before the BA region (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A,E

claim: All cells expressing Fn1 are also DAF-FMDA-positive
source: To better characterize the smooth muscle identity and their activity, we performed a DAF-FMDA assay and counterstained with Fn1 at 72 hpf, 96 hpf and 120 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). These results suggest that all cells expressing Fn1 are also DAF-FMDA-positive (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by DAF-FMDA assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Some of the Fn1-expressing cells also express Tg(wt1a:GFP), a marker of epicardial cells
source: Some of these cells also express Tg(wt1a:GFP) (asterisks in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) a marker of epicardial cells (Peralta et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by transgenic line data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citation to Peralta et al., 2013

claim: The Klf2a reporter is specifically activated in the OFT endothelium from 72 hpf to 120 hpf
source: We could observe a specific activation of the Klf2a reporter in the OFT endothelium (Figure 4A,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), in particular in the ventricular part of the valve (posterior) from 72 hpf to 120 hpf (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 4A,C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The Notch reporter Tg(tp1:dGFP) is specifically expressed in the OFT endothelium in the ventricular part of the valve from 72 hpf to 120 hpf
source: Similarly, the Notch reporter Tg(tp1:dGFP) is specifically expressed in the OFT endothelium (Figure 4B,C), in the ventricular part of the valve from 72 hpf to 120 hpf (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 4B,C,D

claim: The transgene activation is stronger in the posterior part of the valve than the anterior part throughout valve maturation for both Klf2a and Notch reporters
source: Interestingly, the spatial activation of the reporter varies within the valve forming area - the transgene activation is stronger in the posterior part of the valve than the anterior part of the valve throughout the process of valve maturation (Figure 4C,D). We made similar observations for the Notch reporter (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Yap1 is localized in the heart at 72 hpf, in particular in the OFT smooth muscle cells
source: We found that Yap1 is localized in the heart at 72 hpf, in particular in the OFT smooth muscle cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The smooth muscle cells surrounding the OFT and some OFT endothelial cells express Yap1
source: To better characterize its tissue-specific expression, we used the double transgenic line Tg(fli:lifeact-EGFP; kdrl:nls-mCherry) and could show that the smooth muscle cells surrounding the OFT, but also some OFT endothelial cells express Yap1 (asterisks in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data on transgenic line shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The Yap/Wwtr1-Tead reporter was activated in the OFT endothelial cells as well as the smooth muscle cells surrounding the OFT
source: To assess the activity of the Hippo pathway in the heart at 72 hpf, we made use of the Tg(4xGTIIC:d2GFP) and could see that the Yap/Wwtr1-Tead reporter was activated in the OFT endothelial cells (labelled using the kdrl:membrane-mCherry line) as well as the smooth muscle cells surrounding the OFT (labelled by the Elnb staining) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 5A

claim: A significant fraction of yap1-/- embryos displayed abnormal valves (17% at 72 hpf, 8% at 96 hpf, 17% at 120 hpf)
source: When analyzed from 72 hpf until 120 hpf, a significant fraction of yap1-/- embryos displayed abnormal valves (17% at 72 hpf, 8% at 96 hpf, 17% at 120 hpf, n = 12) and an increasing fraction of yap1 embryos did not have recognizable OFT valves (58% at 120hpf, n = 12).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mutant analysis

claim: 58% of yap1 embryos did not have recognizable OFT valves at 120 hpf
source: When analyzed from 72 hpf until 120 hpf, a significant fraction of yap1-/- embryos displayed abnormal valves (17% at 72 hpf, 8% at 96 hpf, 17% at 120 hpf, n = 12) and an increasing fraction of yap1 embryos did not have recognizable OFT valves (58% at 120hpf, n = 12).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mutant analysis

claim: Yap1 is involved during OFT valve morphogenesis
source: Thus, these results suggest that yap1 is involved during OFT valve morphogenesis (Figure 5B) and that smooth muscle cell progenitors are likely to play a role in the process.
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In the group of 'beating heart' embryos (group1), stronger GFP expression is observed in the posterior part of the valve for both Klf2a and Notch reporters at every stage analyzed
source: In the group of 'beating heart' embryos (group1, Video 1), we still observe stronger GFP expression in the posterior part of the valve for both reporters at every stage analyzed (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tnnt2a morpholino experiments shown in Figure 6A

claim: In the group of embryos where the heart is beating at an abnormal slow rate (group2), no difference is observed between the anterior and posterior part of the valve for the Klf2a reporter at 72 hpf
source: In the group of embryos where the heart is still beating but at an abnormal slow rate (less than 2 Hz, group2, Video 2), we observe no difference between the anterior and posterior part of the valve (p=0.99) for the Klf2a reporter at 72 hpf (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tnnt2a morpholino experiments shown in Figure 6B

claim: For the Notch reporter, no difference in fluorescence intensity is observed at 72 hpf in the 'slow beating heart' group
source: For the Notch reporter, we observed no difference in fluorescence intensity at 72 hpf (p=0.1) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tnnt2a morpholino experiments shown in Figure 6B

claim: Fn1, Elnb, and Yap1 are down-regulated in the smooth muscle cells of the 'slow beating heart' embryos
source: In addition, we analyzed the localization of Fn1, Elnb and Yap1 by immunostaining in both 'beating heart' (n = 4, n = 7 and n = 7, respectively) and 'slow beating heart' (n = 6, n = 7 and n = 7 respectively) groups and could observe that Fn1, Elnb, and Yap1 are down-regulated in the smooth muscle cells of the 'slow beating heart' embryos (Figure 6D,F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D,F

claim: The 'slow beating heart' group has a smaller BA
source: Moreover, we assessed the BA diameter and the activity of the smooth muscle using the DAF-FMDA assay (Figure 6E). The results suggest that the 'slow beating heart' group has a smaller BA (p<0,001) and the smooth muscle are much less active (p=0,05) (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E,F

claim: The smooth muscle are much less active in the 'slow beating heart' group
source: Moreover, we assessed the BA diameter and the activity of the smooth muscle using the DAF-FMDA assay (Figure 6E). The results suggest that the 'slow beating heart' group has a smaller BA (p<0,001) and the smooth muscle are much less active (p=0,05) (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by DAF-FMDA assay data shown in Figure 6E,F

claim: All the tnnt2aMO-injected embryos with almost no contraction have no valve
source: We next assessed valve morphology in which blood flow is altered due to slow heart contraction and selected the fish with almost no contraction (group2). All the tnnt2aMO-injected embryos have no valve (n = 9/9, p<10−6) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tnnt2a morpholino experiments shown in Figure 6C

claim: More than 80% of vlad tepes mutant embryos displayed abnormal OFT valves
source: To confirm the role of flow in the process, we analyzed the effect of altered blood viscosity and shear stress by lowering red blood cell content in the gata1 mutants (Vlad Tepes) as previously described (Steed et al., 2016b; Vermot et al., 2009). In vlad tepes mutant embryos (n = 21, p<10−2), more than 80% of the mutants displayed abnormal OFT valves (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 6C and citations to Steed et al., 2016b; Vermot et al., 2009

claim: Most of the klf2a-/- embryos display proper valves at 72 hpf (n = 7/12), 96 hpf (n = 6/12) and 120 hpf (n = 6/12)
source: We found that most of the klf2a-/- embryos display proper valves at 72 hpf (n = 7/12), 96 hpf (n = 6/12) and 120 hpf (n = 6/12).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: 33% of the klf2a-/- embryos have abnormal 'delayed phenotype' at 72 hpf (n = 4/12), at 96 hpf (n = 4/12) and 120 hpf (n = 4/12)
source: However, 33% of the klf2a-/- embryos have abnormal 'delayed phenotype' at 72 hpf (n = 4/12), at 96 hpf (n = 4/12) and 120 hpf (n = 4/12) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 7A

claim: 30% of the notch1b-/- embryos have a 'delayed phenotype' at 72 hpf, 35% at 96 hpf and 45% at 120 hpf
source: In addition, notch1b is also necessary for proper valve formation since 30% (n = 6/20) of the notch1b-/- embryos have a 'delayed phenotype' at 72 hpf, 35% (n = 7/20) at 96 hpf and 45% (n = 9/20) at 120 hpf (Figure 7B) while almost all control embryos have proper valves at 72 hpf (n = 6/7), 96 hpf (n = 7/7) and 120 hpf (n = 7/7) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 7B

claim: In klf2a-/- embryos, notch1b expression is altered with no clear expression defining the OFT region at 48 hpf (64%) and at 72 hpf (78%)
source: In controls, 85% and 91% of the embryos have notch1b expression in the OFT at 48 hpf and 72 hpf, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C). However, in klf2a-/- embryos, notch1b expression is altered with no clear expression defining the OFT region at 48 hpf (64%) and at 72 hpf (78%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C

claim: Most of the embryos show proper klf2a expression in notch1b-/- embryos (61% at 48 hpf and 51% at 72 hpf)
source: However, in the reverse experiment, most of the embryos show proper klf2a expression in notch1b -/- embryos (61% at 48 hpf and 51% at 72 hpf) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: The Notch reporter is significantly more expressed in the posterior part compared to the anterior part of the valves at 72 hpf (p<10−2), 96 hpf (p<10−2) and 120 hpf (p<10−1) in the klf2a+/+ embryos
source: As for Notch reporter expression in wild-type (Figure 4C,D), the Notch reporter is significantly more expressed in the posterior part compared to the anterior part of the valves at 72 hpf (p<10−2), 96 hpf (p<10−2) and 120 hpf (p<10−1) (Figure 7C,C') in the klf2a+/+ embryos.
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 7C,C'

claim: The fluorescent intensity in the posterior part of the valve is significantly reduced in the klf2a-/- compared to klf2a+/+ at 72 hpf (p<10–1), 96 hpf (p<10−1) and 120 hpf (p<10−1)
source: Interestingly, the stronger posterior expression is lost in the klf2a-/- embryos and the fluorescent intensity in the posterior part of the valve is significantly reduced in the klf2a-/- compared to klf2a+/+ at 72 hpf (p<10–1), 96 hpf (p<10−1) and 120 hpf (p<10−1) (Figure 7C,C').
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 7C,C'

claim: The expression in the posterior part of the valve in the notch1b-/- embryos compared to the notch1b+/+ control embryos is not significantly different at any time point analyzed
source: In comparison, the expression in the posterior part of the valve in the notch1b-/- embryos compared to the notch1b+/+ control embryos is not significantly different at any time point analyzed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: Fn1, Elnb, and Yap1 are properly localized in controls and klf2a-/- embryos
source: To further assess whether Klf2 has an effect on the OFT formation, we performed Fn1, Elnb and Yap1 stainings on klf2a-/- and controls at 72 hpf. We could observe that Fn1, Elnb, and Yap1 are properly localized in controls (n = 13/13, n = 7/7 and n = 4/4, respectively), klf2a-/- (n = 5/6, n = 3/4, and n = 3/3) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E

claim: Heart function in trpp2, trpv4, piezo1, and piezo2a mutants is normal based on relative fractional shortening measurements
source: First, we evaluated the relative fractional shortening (RFS) at 72hpf in the atrium and in the ventricle of each mutant and their corresponding controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A). We did not observe any significant difference in the RFS between mutants and their respective controls neither in the atrium nor in the ventricle, suggesting that heart function in these mutants is normal.
evidence: Supported by RFS measurement data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A

claim: The retrograde flow fraction and time windows for forward, reverse or no flow are equivalent in all mutants when compared to their respective controls
source: As another readout of flow forces and heart function, we quantified the retrograde flow fraction (RFF) at 72hpf and 120hpf in these mutants and the time windows for forward, reverse or no flow. We found that they are equivalent in all mutants when compared to their respective controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), confirming that heart function is not different in these mutants.
evidence: Supported by RFF measurement data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B

claim: 33% of the trpv4 mutant embryos have normal valves and mainly display thick valves (67%)
source: We found that 33% of the trpv4 mutant embryos (n = 7) have normal valves and mainly display thick valves (67%).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: In the trpp2 mutant embryos, only 10% have normal valves and 35% are delayed with respect to valve phenotype
source: In the trpp2 mutant embryos (n = 20), a stronger phenotype is observed with only 10% of normal valves. We observed that some embryos are delayed with respect to valve phenotype, meaning that the valve forming area still displays cushions at 120 hpf instead of having leaflets (35%).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: The trpv4-/-; trpp2+/- has an intermediate phenotype with 25% of the embryos having normal valves
source: The trpv4-/-; trpp2+/- (n = 8) has an intermediate phenotype with 25% of the embryos having normal valves.
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: The trpp2-/-; trpv4-/- embryos have a stronger phenotype, with none of the embryos showing proper OFT valve development and displaying mainly a delayed valve phenotype (45%)
source: Finally, the trpp2-/-; trpv4-/- embryos (n = 11) have a stronger phenotype, with none of the embryos showing proper OFT valve development and displaying mainly a delayed valve phenotype (45%).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: The piezo1 mutant embryos show mainly a delayed valve formation (50%)
source: Interestingly, the piezo1 mutant embryos (n = 14) show mainly a delayed valve formation (50%), similarly to the trpv4-/-; trpp2-/- embryos.
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: The piezo2a-/- has a less stringent phenotype with mainly normal valves (44%) but 11% do not have valves at all
source: The piezo2a-/- (n = 9) has a less stringent phenotype with mainly normal valves (44%) but nevertheless 11% of piezo2a-/- fish do not have valves at all.
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: In piezo1-/-; piezo2a-/- embryos, none of the fish display proper valve development and most of them do not form any valves (36%)
source: This phenotype is even more prevalent in piezo1-/-; piezo2a-/- embryos (n = 11), where none of the fish display proper valve development and most of them do not form any valves (36%).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data

claim: trpp2-/- embryos display mainly thick valves at all time points (n = 4/8 at 72 hpf, n = 8/13 at 96 hpf and n = 5/11 at 120 hpf)
source: trpp2-/- embryos display mainly thick valves at all time points (n = 4/8 at 72 hpf, n = 8/13 at 96 hpf and n = 5/11 at 120 hpf) (Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A

claim: piezo1-/- embryos have mainly normal valves at 72 hpf (n = 6/10), display a delayed phenotype at 96 hpf (n = 4/10) and thick or delayed phenotype at 120 hpf (n = 3/10 and n = 3/10 respectively)
source: Although piezo1-/- embryos have mainly normal valves at 72 hpf (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) (n = 6/10), they display a delayed phenotype (still cushions) at 96 hpf (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2) (n = 4/10) and thick or delayed phenotype at 120 hpf (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) (n = 3/10 and n = 3/10 respectively).
evidence: Supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 8A–C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A

claim: A bit more than two thirds of piezo1-/- embryos (n = 7/10) display reduced Yap1 expression
source: A bit more than two thirds of piezo1-/- embryos (n = 7/10) display reduced Yap1 expression as well as a down-regulation of Elnb (n = 9/12) and Fn1 (n = 3/4) (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8E

claim: The BA diameter as well as the DAF-FMDA fluorescence intensity are not affected in the piezo1-/- compared to piezo1+/+
source: However, the BA diameter as well as the DAF-FMDA fluorescence intensity are not affected in the piezo1-/- compared to piezo1+/+ (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) demonstrating that smooth muscle cells are still present in the piezo mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B

claim: Klf2a expression was misregulated in piezo1-/- mutant embryos with stronger Klf2a reporter activation in the anterior and posterior part of the valve endothelium when compared to controls
source: We next assessed Klf2a reporter expression in piezo1-/- and trpp2-/-. We found that Klf2a expression was misregulated in piezo1-/- mutant embryos with stronger Klf2a reporter activation in the anterior and posterior part of the valve endothelium when compared to controls (p<10−3 for the anterior part and p<10−2 for the posterior part of the valves) (Figure 8F,F').
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 8F,F'

claim: The posterior part of the valve has a decreased expression of GFP in trpp2-/- embryos, highlighting a down-regulation of klf2a
source: By contrast, we found that the posterior part of the valve has a decreased expression of GFP (p<10−2), highlighting a down-regulation of klf2a in the trpp2-/- embryos (Figure 8G,G').
evidence: Supported by reporter line data shown in Figure 8G,G'

claim: trpp2 is ubiquitously expressed in the embryo, including in the different layers composing the OFT
source: To assess if the localization of piezo1 and trpp2 mRNA could explain the differential function of these channels, we performed RNAscope assay at 72hpf (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A). We found that trpp2 is ubiquitously expressed in the embryo, including in the different layers composing the OFT.
evidence: Supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A

claim: piezo1 is expressed in both endothelium and smooth muscles, albeit at a lower level than trpp2
source: Similarly, we found that piezo1 is expressed in both endothelium and smooth muscles, albeit at a lower level than trpp2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A

claim: The piezo1:nls-Venus reporter is expressed mostly in smooth muscles at 72hpf and cells of the endothelium of the OFT valve
source: To confirm these results, we generated a transgenic reporter line with 3 kb of the piezo1 promoter upstream of the start codon (piezo1:nls-Venus). We observed the expression of the reporter line mostly in smooth muscles at 72hpf (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B) and cells of the endothelium of the OFT valve.
evidence: Supported by transgenic reporter line data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B

claim: Trpp2 is expressed in the endothelium and the smooth muscles
source: Trpp2 immunohistochemistry showed that Trpp2 is expressed in the endothelium and the smooth muscles confirming that trpp2 is ubiquitously expressed in the OFT (arrow in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B

claim: Piezo1 plays a dual role in the OFT: it modulates klf2a expression in the endothelium and it is necessary for proper smooth muscle cell maturation around the OFT endothelium
source: We conclude that Piezo1 plays a dual role in the OFT: it modulates klf2a expression in the endothelium and it is necessary for proper smooth muscle cell maturation around the OFT endothelium.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing Piezo1's effects on both klf2a expression and smooth muscle markers

claim: OFT valve formation proceeds via an initial stage of endothelial cell folding associated with the generation of a cluster of smooth muscle cell progenitors surrounding the endothelial layer
source: We show that OFT valve formation proceeds via an initial stage of endothelial cell folding, which is associated with the generation of a cluster of smooth muscle cell progenitors surrounding the endothelial layer.
evidence: Based on experimental data from photoconversion and immunostaining experiments

claim: Notch and Klf2 are key flow-dependent factors necessary for the correct coordination of OFT valvulogenesis
source: Using live reporters to highlight the signaling changes accompanying these temporally coordinated cell-movement events and genetics, we identified Notch and Klf2 as key flow-dependent factors as well as Yap1 as necessary factors for the correct coordination of OFT valvulogenesis.
evidence: Based on reporter line data and mutant analysis showing flow-dependent expression and requirement for valve formation

claim: Yap1 is a necessary factor for the correct coordination of OFT valvulogenesis
source: Using live reporters to highlight the signaling changes accompanying these temporally coordinated cell-movement events and genetics, we identified Notch and Klf2 as key flow-dependent factors as well as Yap1 as necessary factors for the correct coordination of OFT valvulogenesis.
evidence: Based on mutant analysis showing Yap1 requirement for valve formation

claim: Piezo and Trp channels are key regulators of klf2 activity in the endothelium
source: We show that Piezo and Trp channels are key regulators of klf2 activity in the endothelium and that piezo modulates Yap1 localization in the smooth muscle cells, providing a molecular link between mechanosensitivity and cell signaling in the multilayered valve structure.
evidence: Based on mutant analysis showing effects on klf2 reporter expression

claim: Piezo modulates Yap1 localization in the smooth muscle cells
source: We show that Piezo and Trp channels are key regulators of klf2 activity in the endothelium and that piezo modulates Yap1 localization in the smooth muscle cells, providing a molecular link between mechanosensitivity and cell signaling in the multilayered valve structure.
evidence: Based on immunostaining data showing reduced Yap1 expression in piezo1 mutants

claim: The tissue remodeling occurring during OFT valve development is significantly different from AVC valve development where the endocardium is the main remodeling tissue
source: We conclude that the tissue remodeling occurring during OFT valve development is significantly different from AVC valve development where the endocardium is the main remodeling tissue (Beis et al., 2005; Pestel et al., 2016; Steed et al., 2016b).
evidence: Based on photoconversion data showing folding without multilayering and citations to Beis et al., 2005; Pestel et al., 2016; Steed et al., 2016b

claim: Klf2a and Notch signaling are activated specifically in the part of the valve corresponding to where the OFT has the smallest diameter and where shear stress is expected to be the highest
source: These results suggest that Klf2a and Notch signaling are activated specifically in the part of the valve corresponding to where the OFT has the smallest diameter and where shear stress is expected to be the highest, consistent with the hypothesis that Klf2a and Notch signaling are flow-responsive.
evidence: Based on reporter line data showing stronger expression in posterior part of valve and inference about shear stress

claim: The expression of both Klf2a and Notch reporters is flow-dependent
source: Together, these results suggest that the expression of both Klf2a and Notch reporters is flow-dependent and that mechanical forces associated with heart activity are necessary for valve development and smooth muscle cell identity in the OFT.
evidence: Based on tnnt2a morpholino experiments showing altered reporter expression with reduced heart contraction

claim: Mechanical forces associated with heart activity are necessary for valve development and smooth muscle cell identity in the OFT
source: Together, these results suggest that the expression of both Klf2a and Notch reporters is flow-dependent and that mechanical forces associated with heart activity are necessary for valve development and smooth muscle cell identity in the OFT.
evidence: Based on tnnt2a morpholino and vlad tepes mutant experiments showing valve defects and altered smooth muscle markers

claim: klf2a and notch1b are involved for proper valve morphogenesis
source: These results suggest that klf2a and notch1b are involved for proper valve morphogenesis and that Klf2a modulates notch expression in the process.
evidence: Based on mutant analysis showing valve defects in klf2a and notch1b mutants

claim: Klf2a modulates notch expression in the process of valve morphogenesis
source: These results suggest that klf2a and notch1b are involved for proper valve morphogenesis and that Klf2a modulates notch expression in the process.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization and reporter line data showing altered notch expression in klf2a mutants

claim: klf2a does not seem necessary for the smooth muscle cell differentiation surrounding the endothelium
source: Moreover, klf2a does not seem necessary for the smooth muscle cell differentiation surrounding the endothelium.
evidence: Based on immunostaining data showing proper localization of Fn1, Elnb, and Yap1 in klf2a mutants

claim: Piezo1 inhibits klf2a overall the valve endothelium
source: These results suggest that Piezo1 inhibits klf2a overall the valve endothelium (Figure 8F,F') while Trpp2 is required for klf2a activation in the posterior part of the OFT valve endothelium (Figure 8G,G').
evidence: Based on reporter line data showing increased klf2a expression in piezo1 mutants shown in Figure 8F,F'

claim: Trpp2 is required for klf2a activation in the posterior part of the OFT valve endothelium
source: These results suggest that Piezo1 inhibits klf2a overall the valve endothelium (Figure 8F,F') while Trpp2 is required for klf2a activation in the posterior part of the OFT valve endothelium (Figure 8G,G').
evidence: Based on reporter line data showing decreased klf2a expression in trpp2 mutants shown in Figure 8G,G'

claim: Piezo1 is important for tissue remodeling in mouse arteries
source: Piezo function in these two cell layers is consistent with the fact that Piezo1 is expressed in smooth muscle cells and is important for tissue remodeling in mouse arteries (Retailleau et al., 2015) as well as in endothelial cells in mouse vasculature (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014) and lymphatic valves (Nonomura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Retailleau et al., 2015

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in endothelial cells in mouse vasculature
source: Piezo function in these two cell layers is consistent with the fact that Piezo1 is expressed in smooth muscle cells and is important for tissue remodeling in mouse arteries (Retailleau et al., 2015) as well as in endothelial cells in mouse vasculature (Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014) and lymphatic valves (Nonomura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014; Nonomura et al., 2018

claim: Piezo is sensitive to stretch
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the fact that Piezo is sensitive to stretch (Ranade et al., 2015), compression (Lee et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2015), and rhythmic mechanical stimuli (Lewis et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ranade et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2017

claim: Piezo-dependent mechanisms can transduce forces at the cell-cell or cell-matrix interface
source: Importantly, Piezo-dependent mechanisms can transduce forces at the cell-cell or cell-matrix interface (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Poole et al., 2014

claim: Yap1 has been shown to translocate less in the nucleus in Piezo1 mutant mice neural stem cells
source: Interestingly, Yap1 has been shown to translocate less in the nucleus in Piezo1 mutant mice neural stem cells (Pathak et al., 2014) and to induce proliferation in smooth muscles during cardiovascular development in mouse (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2014

claim: Yap1 induces proliferation in smooth muscles during cardiovascular development in mouse
source: Interestingly, Yap1 has been shown to translocate less in the nucleus in Piezo1 mutant mice neural stem cells (Pathak et al., 2014) and to induce proliferation in smooth muscles during cardiovascular development in mouse (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014

claim: In zebrafish, Yap1 is involved in the determination of cardiac precursor cells into smooth muscle cell fate via a process that involves the regulation of Elastinb expression
source: In zebrafish, Yap1 is involved in the determination of cardiac precursor cells into smooth muscle cell fate via a process that involves the regulation of Elastinb expression (Moriyama et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moriyama et al., 2016

claim: Yap1 expression is flow inducible in the vascular system
source: It is thus possible that Piezo acts as a regulator of tissue mechanical properties by regulating Yap1 expression both in the OFT and in the vascular system where Yap1 expression is flow inducible (Nakajima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakajima et al., 2017
